headlines.article_text: S&P 500 correction: What caused the market sell-off Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory Friday, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite is now in the red for 2026. There are five main reasons behind the sell-off including the Anthropic IPO, Nvidia's mounting troubles and a Federal Reserve losing the inflation fight. Wharton finance professor Jeremy Siegel believes the correction is a resetting of expectations after three years of double-digit annual returns for stocks. In this article .SPX NVDA Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT watch now VIDEO 1:03 01:03 Hardly anyone saw this selloff coming, says Wharton Prof. Jeremy Siegel Closing Bell Esteemed Wharton professor Jeremy Siegel was more animated than usual on Friday afternoon... with good reason. The normally staid author of "Stocks for the Long Run" spoke to CNBC on Friday as the market careened toward some ugly milestones. The S&P 500 and Dow Jones Industrial Average closed in correction territory, off more than 10% from their records. The Nasdaq Composite lost its gain for the year and the more concentrated Nasdaq-100 entered bear market territory on an intraday basis. "These things are like straws that break the camel's back. You know what I mean? Everyone [is] all, 'I don't care, I don't care cause everything else is good' and when those straws keep on going... Bang," said Siegel. Nasdaq Composite, YTD Just a month-and-a-half ago, the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq Composite were at record highs. But the straws were already adding up by then and a market in denial is just now recognizing them. Here are the reasons behind the sell-off: 1. Anthropic IPO cash-out The breaking point came this week in the form of the initial public offering of artificial intelligence leader Anthropic and a pick-up in the selling intensity for one-time AI chip leader Nvidia. Anthropic upped its offering amount a day before going public despite the already dimming climate around AI-related stocks. The move ensured it would be the biggest IPO ever, but played into the fears that this debut — following SpaceX's monster offering over the summer — was a collective cash-out moment for the AI complex that will leave the investing masses holding the bag. In other words, it could be the ultimate "sell the news" moment for the AI trade. On Thursday, Anthropic traded from its $83 IPO price to a high above $115 before instantly rolling over and taking the AI trade with it. Anthropic's sell-off intensified Friday, and when the dust settled Anthropic closed the week at $88.91. The Nasdaq posted its worst week since the Covid plunge of March 2020, down 10%. 2. Nvidia's mounting woes Nvidia fell 14% on Friday with the selling intensifying after a Reuters headline hit the tape that the chipmaker's accounting is the focus of a Securities and Exchange Commission probe. Nvidia is now down nearly 40% in November alone, a month that saw the AI bull market's leading salesman, Jensen Huang, resign as its CEO because of an affair with an alleged Chinese spy that raised speculation about whether the company's chips were ending up in Beijing's hands despite government restrictions. To start the week, the Commerce Department tightened restrictions on U.S.-made chips to stop China from accessing them remotely from other countries. A solid earnings report on Tuesday fell flat as Nvidia's board definitively ruled out any chance Huang would return, disappointing some of the stock's fanatics still holding out hope for his far-fetched return. Nvidia ended the week with a 23% loss. Nvidia, 1 month 3. S&P 500 breaks its long-term trend The S&P 500 traded below its 200-day moving average — what's considered a measure of a security's long-term trend — on Tuesday and made a convincing break of it on Thursday. This turned many on Wall Street— like commodity trading advisors — into automatic sellers on the market. So-called CTAs are individuals or organizations that advise others on trading futures and swaps across a range of assets. "We know there's a lot of trend riders on these markets," said Siegel. "They have their trend lines. They've ridden it up and as soon as it goes down, they're selling and they're selling and they're selling and they just perpetuate" the decline, he said. 4. Inflation is forcing the Fed's hand The Iran conflict has caused the price oil to surge and while it's off its highs it still remains above $83 a barrel, while the fees for transiting the Strait of Hormuz and the rest of the region keep persistent pressure on global prices. A series of numbers earlier in the month showed inflation is still far from the Federal Reserve's 2% target, sparking a run of central bank officials to warn they may have to get more aggressive with interest rates. After increasing rates in September by a quarter point, the Fed skipped a hike in late October and sparked concern among bond investors it may be falling behind the inflation fight. The 10-year Treasury yield subsequently jumped above 5% and stayed there until a flight of safe haven fixed income buying brought it back below that level on Friday. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said this week that the Fed may need to do a half percentage point hike next month to catch up. "I'm very, very concerned about inflation. It's kind of headed in the wrong direction, and it's spreading out," Waller told CNBC. "Don't fight the Fed" has long been a maxim on Wall Street and right now expectations are that the central bank will need to raise rates in December and again in January. And late-breaking on Friday was a report from the Financial Times that the Trump Administration is considering restarting strikes on Iran . 5. Pace of earnings growth slowing Before the grim market milestones were met on Friday, it had long lost its mojo on fears that the pace of growth driven by AI companies was slowing. As Anthropic prepared to go public, its third-quarter figures released earlier this month showed revenue growth last quarter was 47%, down from 144% in the second quarter. AI momentum trades, like the VanEck Semiconductor ETF and the iShares MSCI USA Momentum Factor ETF , all topped out during the summer. VanEck Semiconductor ETF (SMH), YTD The fears of slowing growth picked up this month after the Democrats won control of Congress and key governorships, fueling speculation that states — or even the whole country — could implement stricter rules on data center construction. CoreWeave , which builds data centers using high amounts of debt, is down 71% from its high. Caterpillar , which has reinvented itself as an AI play because of data center construction and generators, is down more than 50% from its high. Resetting expectations The view of Siegel and many market observers is that the economy remains in good enough shape that this will just be a run-of-the-mill correction that resets a bull market that had raised people's expectations too high because of its early ferocity. The S&P 500 returned more than 20% in 2023 and 2024 and then gained 16% last year. "The average over long periods for the stock market is 8%, 9% a year up," said Siegel. "People began to think that 15 to 20 [percent] was going to be the norm with AI and we have to bring that down to reality." "Stay with your stocks,' he said. The only problem with that theory is that the stock market and its wealth effect was one of the major factors underpinning the economy. Stocks are a greater source of household wealth — especially for baby boomers — than they ever have been before. With the S&P 500 clinging to a 1% gain for the year, this stock market rout could end up tipping off a virtuous cycle that slows the economy, and in turn, leads to bigger equity losses. headlines.summary: Prime Minister Modi's government says it orders content to be taken down only if it breaches local laws, or can harm public safety or national security.
headlines.article_text: Meta's India offices hit by opposition protests over account removals Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu In this article META Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Patrick Pleul | Picture Alliance | Getty Images The youth wing of India's main opposition Congress party clashed with police outside Meta offices, protesting the company's removal of some Instagram accounts of its members, according to footage released by the group on Saturday. Meta declined to comment on the protests, an escalation by the influential political group in the company's biggest market by users. Debate is growing in India about potential risks to free speech from the increasingly strict efforts of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government to remove social media content it objects to. Modi's government says it orders content taken down only if it breaches local laws, can harm public safety or national security. Congress has long accused Meta and other social media platforms of curbing dissent online by removing party accounts, favoring Modi's government. Meta has said it restricts content in India to comply with local laws. Modi's party accuses Congress of vandalism Pradeep Bhandari, a national spokesperson for Modi's ruling party, criticized Congress' actions on Saturday, saying they had "not only vandalised and destroyed Meta's office in Hyderabad" but were also "flaunting it on social media". "This is Congress Model: Vandalise offices of Private companies," he wrote. India's IT ministry did not immediately respond to requests for comment. In Hyderabad on Friday, protesters carrying placards chanted slogans as they stormed into the building that houses Meta's offices, smashing plants to the ground and clashing with police, according to footage released by the Indian Youth Congress' X account. Another video showed Congress workers spray-painting anti-Meta slogans on walls outside the building that houses its Mumbai office, clashing with security guards who tried to stop them. In Gurugram near New Delhi, Congress workers chanted slogans and held banners reading "restore youth Congress accounts", official online posts showed. The Indian Youth Congress posted warnings on X that it would "storm your offices across the country and stage protests" unless Instagram accounts of its leaders are restored. Two such accounts were restored after Friday's protests, but thousands of accounts of journalists, creators and influencers critical of the government remain restricted, Manu Jain, who is in charge of social media for the youth group, told Reuters on Saturday. Meta must explain how its algorithms restrict posts and must restore accounts taken down on government orders, he added. Reporters Without Borders has said the removal of journalistic content from social media has been on the rise in India this year, and free speech activists say a new government rule gives social media companies hardly any time to review and decide on takedown requests. In February, Modi's government ordered social media companies to take down unlawful content within three hours of being notified about it, tightening an earlier 36-hour timeline. Meta disclosures show that it restricted more than 5.4 million posts or accounts in India under local laws in the first half of 2026, second only to Indonesia and up from about 70,000 in the preceding six months. "The large majority of these items included instances where we were obligated to proactively restrict content ... based on local law requirements," Meta said.
